topics.t: What makes a collection a set
topics.h: Relations, functions, probability, even geometry — all of Class 11 and 12 maths is written in one language: the language of sets.
p: A set is a well-defined collection of objects: for any object, you can decide without doubt whether it belongs or not.
'Rivers of India' is well-defined; 'the five most famous Indian cricketers' is not, because 'most famous' depends on opinion.
Objects in a set are its elements or members. a ∈ A means 'a belongs to A'; b ∉ A means 'b does not belong to A'.
Standard sets: N = natural numbers, Z = integers, Q = rational numbers, R = real numbers; Z⁺, Q⁺, R⁺ are their positive members.
Sets are the base for relations, functions, sequences and probability that you will meet later in this book.

ex.q: Let A = {vowels in the English alphabet}. Fill in ∈ or ∉: (i) e ___ A (ii) b ___ A (iii) u ___ A.
st: The vowels are a, e, i, o, u, so A = {a, e, i, o, u}.
e is a vowel, so e ∈ A.
b is a consonant, so b ∉ A.
u is a vowel, so u ∈ A.
ex.a: e ∈ A, b ∉ A, u ∈ A

topics.rl: The Election Commission's voter list is a set: for any person, the rule 'Indian citizen, 18 or older on the qualifying date and enrolled' decides clearly whether they are in it.

rv.summary: A set is a well-defined collection of objects, so for any object we can say clearly whether it belongs. We write a ∈ A when a belongs to A and b ∉ A when it does not.
focus: Decide whether a collection is well-defined (a set) or depends on opinion
Use ∈ and ∉ correctly between an element and a set
Place numbers in the standard sets N, Z, Q and R
remember: Set: a well-defined collection of objects
a ∈ A: a belongs to A; b ∉ A: b does not belong to A
N = natural numbers, Z = integers, Q = rational numbers, R = real numbers; Z⁺, Q⁺, R⁺ are their positive members
traps: Don't accept words like 'best', 'famous' or 'difficult' in a set's rule: they depend on opinion
Don't put −3 in N or √2 in Q: −3 is an integer but not natural, and √2 is irrational

topics.h: You can describe your class either by reading out every name, or by saying 'all students of 11-B'. Sets have exactly these two styles.
p: Roster (tabular) form lists the elements inside braces, separated by commas: {2, 3, 5, 7}.
In roster form an element is not repeated and the order does not matter: {1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2}.
Set-builder form describes the common property: {x : x is a prime number less than 10}. The colon ':' is read 'such that'.
To convert, either list the elements that satisfy the property, or spot the pattern in a list and write it as a rule.
{1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5} in set-builder form is {x : x = n/(n + 1), n ∈ N and n ≤ 4}.

ex.q: Write A = {x : x is an integer and −3 ≤ x < 2} in roster form.
st: Integers from −3 up to but not including 2.

topics.rl: An IRCTC filter such as 'all trains from Delhi to Mumbai leaving after 6 pm' is a set-builder description; the list of trains it shows is the roster form.

rv.summary: A set can be written in roster form, listing its distinct elements in braces, or in set-builder form, stating the property its elements share, like {x : x is prime, x < 10}.
focus: Convert set-builder form to roster form by listing the elements that satisfy the rule
Convert a roster list into set-builder form by spotting the pattern, with the correct range of n
Write each element once; order does not matter
remember: Roster form: {2, 3, 5, 7}; elements not repeated, order does not matter
Set-builder form: {x : property}; ':' is read 'such that'
traps: Don't repeat letters or numbers in roster form: BANANA gives {B, A, N}
Don't forget to limit n in set-builder form, or the set becomes infinite

topics.h: A set of even primes greater than 2? Empty. The set of grains of sand on Marina Beach? Huge — but still finite!
p: The empty (null or void) set has no elements. It is written ∅ or { }.
A rule that no object satisfies gives ∅, e.g. {x : x ∈ R and x² = −1} or {x : x is a natural number, 1 < x < 2}.
A set is finite if it is empty or its elements can be counted with a last number; n(A) is the number of elements. n(∅) = 0.
A set that is not finite is infinite, e.g. N, the points on a line, or the lines through a point.
Infinite sets in roster form use dots: N = {1, 2, 3, …}, Z = {…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …}. Some infinite sets, like R, cannot be listed at all.

ex.q: Classify as finite or infinite: (i) {x : x ∈ N and (x − 1)(x − 2) = 0} (ii) the set of multiples of 5 (iii) the set of circles through the origin.
st: (i) x = 1 or 2, both natural, so the set is {1, 2}: finite.
(iii) We can draw circles of any radius through the origin: infinite.

topics.rl: The set of Indian Railways stations is finite (about 7,000+), even though it is large. Finite only means it can be counted to an end.

rv.summary: The empty set ∅ has no elements. A set is finite if it is empty or its elements can be counted to a last number, with n(A) elements; otherwise it is infinite, like N or Z.
focus: Recognise rules that no object satisfies, giving ∅
Classify sets as finite or infinite
Write infinite sets in roster form using dots, and find n(A) for finite sets
remember: Empty set: ∅ or { }, with n(∅) = 0
Finite set: empty, or its elements can be counted with a last number; n(A) = number of elements
traps: {0} is not empty: it has one element, 0
'Very large' or 'hard to count' is not the same as infinite

topics.h: Every Virat Kohli fan in your class is also a cricket fan — so the set of Kohli fans sits inside the set of cricket fans. That is a subset.
p: A = B when they have exactly the same elements. Repetition and order do not matter: {1, 2, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2}.
Sets with the same number of elements are equivalent; they need not be equal. {1, 2, 3} and {a, b, c} are equivalent, not equal.
A ⊆ B (A is a subset of B) if every element of A is in B. Then B is a superset of A.
If A ⊆ B and A ≠ B, A is a proper subset: A ⊂ B. Every set is a subset of itself, and ∅ is a subset of every set.
A = B exactly when A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A — the standard way to prove two sets are equal.

ex.q: Is A = {x : x is a letter of the word FOLLOW} equal to B = {x : x is a letter of the word WOLF}?
st: Letters of FOLLOW: F, O, L, W (repeats dropped).
Letters of WOLF: W, O, L, F.
ex.a: Yes, A = B = {F, O, L, W}

topics.rl: An RBI list of scheduled banks contains the list of public sector banks: every public sector bank is a scheduled bank, so it is a subset.

rv.summary: Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements. A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B; a proper subset A ⊂ B is a subset that is not equal to B.
focus: Decide whether two sets are equal, or only equivalent (same number of elements)
Check A ⊆ B element by element and identify proper subsets
Tell an element (∈) apart from a subset (⊂)
Use A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A to prove A = B
remember: A = B when they have exactly the same elements; repetition and order do not matter
A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B; A ⊂ B: A ⊆ B and A ≠ B
Every set is a subset of itself, and ∅ is a subset of every set
A = B exactly when A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A
traps: Equivalent sets are not always equal: {1, 2, 3} and {a, b, c} are equivalent, not equal
Don't write {a} ∈ {a, b, c}: {a} is a subset, a is the element

topics.t: Listing subsets and the number-system chain
topics.h: Pick toppings for a dosa from {cheese, paneer}: none, cheese only, paneer only or both. Those four choices are exactly the subsets!
p: A singleton set has exactly one element, e.g. {0} or {x : x ∈ N, x² = 4} = {2}.
To list all subsets, go by size: ∅, then one-element sets, then two-element sets, and so on up to the set itself.
Number systems form a chain: N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R. The irrationals T = R − Q satisfy T ⊂ R, and T is not a subset of Q.
Use ∈ between an element and a set, and ⊂ between two sets. {3} ⊂ {1, 3} but 3 ∈ {1, 3}.

ex.q: List all the subsets of A = {1, {1}}.
st: The elements are 1 and {1} — two elements.

topics.rl: A food-delivery app filter with 3 on/off options (veg, offers, fast delivery) can be set in 8 different ways — one for each subset of the 3 options.

rv.summary: A singleton set has exactly one element. Subsets can be listed by size, from ∅ up to the set itself; the number systems form the chain N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R, with irrationals T ⊂ R.
focus: List all subsets of a small set in order of size
Count subsets and proper subsets of sets with 1, 2 or 3 elements
Use ∈ for an element and ⊂ for a subset, even when elements are themselves sets
Place numbers in N, Z, Q, T and R
remember: {a} has 2 subsets, {a, b} has 4, {1, 2, 3} has 8
N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R; T = R − Q (irrationals), T ⊂ R, T is not a subset of Q
traps: Don't count the set itself as a proper subset
Don't confuse an element {3, 4} of a set with a subset

topics.h: A pass mark rule like 'score at least 33 but less than 100' is an interval — and writing it with the right bracket is the whole game.
p: Open interval (a, b) = {x : a < x < b}: end points NOT included.
Closed interval [a, b] = {x : a ≤ x ≤ b}: both end points included.
Half-open: [a, b) = {x : a ≤ x < b} and (a, b] = {x : a < x ≤ b}.
On the number line, a filled dot means the end point is included; a hollow dot means it is excluded.
The length of each of these intervals is b − a, whether it is open, closed or half-open.

ex.q: Write {x : x ∈ R, −4 < x ≤ 6} as an interval and find its length.

topics.rl: IMD issues a heat-wave alert when temperature is in a band like [40 °C, 45 °C) — a half-open interval in action.

rv.summary: Intervals are subsets of R: (a, b) leaves out both end points, [a, b] includes both, and [a, b) or (a, b] include only one. Every such interval has length b − a.
focus: Convert between set-builder inequalities and interval notation
Decide which end points belong to an interval
Show intervals on a number line with filled or hollow dots
Compare intervals and find their length
remember: Filled dot: end point included; hollow dot: end point excluded
Length of the interval = b − a
traps: Don't use '(' with ≤: ≤ includes the end point and needs '['
An interval contains all real numbers in the range, not just whole numbers

topics.h: Talking about IPL players? Your 'universe' is all IPL players — not all humans. Choosing the right universal set keeps every question sharp.
p: The universal set U is the basic set of a context; all sets under discussion are its subsets.
Different contexts need different U: for N, Z and Q, U can be R; for triangles, U can be the set of all polygons or all triangles.
U need not be unique, but it must contain every set being discussed.
In a Venn diagram (after John Venn), U is a rectangle and its subsets are circles (or ovals) inside it.
If A ⊂ B, the circle of A is drawn completely inside the circle of B; elements are shown as points in the right region.

ex.q: Choose a universal set for A = {1, 3, 5}, B = {2, 4, 6} and C = {0, 2, 4, 6, 8}.
st: U must contain every element of A, B and C.
{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} works; so does the set of whole numbers.
ex.a: U = {0, 1, 2, …, 8} (or any larger set such as W)

topics.rl: The census uses U = all residents of India, with circles for 'urban', 'literate', 'working' — a giant Venn diagram of the nation.

rv.summary: The universal set U is the basic set of a context, containing every set under discussion. In a Venn diagram U is a rectangle and its subsets are circles inside it.
focus: Choose a suitable universal set that contains every given set
Read and draw Venn diagrams, including A ⊂ B
Place an element in the correct region of a Venn diagram
remember: Universal set U: all sets under discussion are subsets of U
U need not be unique, but it must contain every set being discussed
Venn diagram (John Venn): U is a rectangle, subsets are circles inside it
traps: U does not have to equal A ∪ B; it can be larger
If A ⊂ B, draw A's circle inside B's, not the other way round

topics.h: Your friends who play cricket OR football form a union; those who play both form the intersection. Same people, two very different questions.
p: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}. Its Venn region is everything inside either circle.
Union laws: A ∪ B = B ∪ A; (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C); A ∪ ∅ = A; A ∪ A = A; U ∪ A = U.
A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}: only the overlap. If A ∩ B = ∅, A and B are disjoint.
Intersection laws: commutative, associative, A ∩ ∅ = ∅, A ∩ U = A, A ∩ A = A.
Distributive law: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).

st: A ∩ (B ∪ C): elements of A in that set = {3, 4}.
Check with distributive law: A ∩ B = {3, 4}, A ∩ C = {4}; union = {3, 4}.

topics.rl: A bank's KYC team keeps 'customers with PAN' ∩ 'customers with Aadhaar linked' to find fully verified accounts.

rv.summary: A ∪ B contains every element in A or B, and A ∩ B contains only elements in both. If A ∩ B = ∅ the sets are disjoint; union and intersection follow commutative, associative and distributive laws.
focus: Find A ∪ B and A ∩ B in roster form
Identify disjoint sets
Use the laws: A ∪ ∅ = A, A ∩ ∅ = ∅, A ∩ U = A, A ∪ U = U
Describe A ∪ B ('or') and A ∩ B ('and') in words
remember: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}; A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}
A ∩ B = ∅ means A and B are disjoint
A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) (distributive law)
traps: Don't write common elements twice in a union
Don't mix up the laws: A ∩ ∅ = ∅ (not A) and A ∪ U = U (not A)

topics.h: Students who passed Maths but NOT Physics: that's A − B, the set that tells the teacher who needs Physics revision.
p: A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}: elements of A that are not in B.
A − B, A ∩ B and B − A are pairwise disjoint, and their union is A ∪ B.
With intervals, think on the number line: [0, 5] − (2, 7) = [0, 2].
A − B = A ∩ B′ when a universal set is fixed (B′ is the complement of B).

ex.q: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, B = {2, 4, 6, 8}. Find A − B, B − A and check that A − B, A ∩ B, B − A make up A ∪ B.
st: A − B: in A, not in B = {1, 3, 5}.
B − A: in B, not in A = {8}.
ex.a: A − B = {1, 3, 5}, B − A = {8}; the three parts are disjoint and form A ∪ B

topics.rl: A startup compares 'users who installed the app' − 'users who made a purchase' to find people to send a discount coupon.

rv.summary: A − B contains the elements of A that are not in B, and in general A − B ≠ B − A. The parts A − B, A ∩ B and B − A are disjoint and together make A ∪ B.
focus: Find A − B and B − A in roster form
Find differences of intervals using the number line
Use the facts that A − B, A ∩ B and B − A are pairwise disjoint and form A ∪ B
remember: A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}
In general A − B ≠ B − A
A − B = A ∩ B′ when a universal set is fixed
traps: Don't take elements from B when finding A − B: start with A only
Watch the end points: [−2, 8) − [0, 10] = [−2, 0), because 0 is removed

topics.h: 'Not (tea or coffee)' means 'no tea AND no coffee'. That everyday logic is De Morgan's law in disguise.
p: Complement of A: A′ = U − A = {x : x ∈ U and x ∉ A}. In a Venn diagram it is the region of U outside A.
Complement laws: A ∪ A′ = U, A ∩ A′ = ∅, (A′)′ = A, U′ = ∅, ∅′ = U.
De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
Describe complements in words: if U = all triangles and A = equilateral triangles, A′ = triangles that are not equilateral.
To prove identities, use laws step by step or Venn diagrams. Example: A ∩ B = A ⇔ A ⊆ B; and A − B = A ∩ B′.
topics.rl: In a cricket survey, U = all fans; 'fans who watch neither Test nor T20' is (Test ∪ T20)′ = Test′ ∩ T20′.

rv.summary: The complement A′ = U − A contains everything in U that is not in A. De Morgan's laws say (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
focus: Find A′ in roster form or describe it in words
Use the complement laws A ∪ A′ = U, A ∩ A′ = ∅, (A′)′ = A
State and verify De Morgan's laws
Recognise A ∩ B = A ⇔ A ⊆ B and A − B = A ∩ B′
remember: A′ = U − A = {x : x ∈ U and x ∉ A}
(A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′
traps: Don't forget to flip ∪ and ∩ in De Morgan's laws
A′ depends on U: always take elements from U, not from outside it

topics.h: A seat in a cinema is 'Row F, Seat 12' — not 'Seat F, Row 12'. Order matters, and that is the heart of an ordered pair.
p: Relations and functions are built by pairing elements of one set with elements of another.
An ordered pair (a, b) has a first and a second element. (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d. So (2, 3) ≠ (3, 2).
Cartesian product: A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}. If A or B is ∅, then A × B = ∅.
If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A × B) = pq.
In general A × B ≠ B × A; they are equal only when A = B (or one of them is empty).

st: Equate first elements: x/3 + 1 = 5/3, so x/3 = 2/3 and x = 2.
Equate second elements: y − 2/3 = 1/3, so y = 1.

topics.rl: A pizza menu with 4 bases and 3 toppings offers 4 × 3 = 12 pizza combinations — every (base, topping) ordered pair of a Cartesian product.

rv.summary: An ordered pair (a, b) has a fixed first and second element, and A × B is the set of all pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A × B) = pq.
focus: Write A × B by pairing every element of A (first) with every element of B (second)
Use equality of ordered pairs to find unknowns
Count n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B)
Know when A × B = B × A and that A × ∅ = ∅
remember: (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d
A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}
n(A × B) = pq when n(A) = p and n(B) = q
traps: (2, 3) ≠ (3, 2): order matters in an ordered pair
Don't add n(A) and n(B): n(A × B) is their product

topics.t: Triplets and reading back the sets
topics.h: A drone over Bengaluru needs three numbers — latitude-style x, y and height z. That is an ordered triplet from R × R × R.
p: A × A × A = {(a, b, c) : a, b, c ∈ A}; each (a, b, c) is an ordered triplet.
R × R is the coordinate plane (all points (x, y)); R × R × R is three-dimensional space.
If n(A) = k, then n(A × A) = k² and n(A × A × A) = k³.
To recover A and B from A × B: collect all first elements to get A and all second elements to get B.
If only some elements of A × B are given, A must contain all their first elements and B all their second elements.

ex.q: A × B = {(p, q), (p, r), (m, q), (m, r)}. Find A and B.
st: First elements: p, m, so A = {p, m}.
Second elements: q, r, so B = {q, r}.

topics.rl: ISRO tracks a satellite with three coordinates at each instant — every position is an ordered triplet in R × R × R.

rv.summary: An ordered triplet (a, b, c) is an element of A × A × A. If n(A) = k then n(A × A) = k² and n(A × A × A) = k³; from A × B, the first elements give A and the second elements give B.
focus: Count elements of A × A and A × A × A
Recover A and B from a listed A × B
Find A from part of A × A and its size
Know that R × R is the plane and R × R × R is space
remember: n(A × A) = k² and n(A × A × A) = k³ when n(A) = k
A = set of first elements of A × B; B = set of second elements
R × R = coordinate plane; R × R × R = three-dimensional space
traps: Don't mix up (1, 4) ∈ A × B with (4, 1): the first entry must come from the first set
Don't count repeated first elements twice when finding n(A)

topics.h: 'Is a student of' links names to schools; 'is the capital of' links cities to states. Every such link is a relation — a chosen subset of a Cartesian product.
p: A relation R from A to B is any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R, b is the image of a and a is a pre-image of b.
Domain = set of first elements of R; codomain = B; range = set of second elements (images). Range ⊆ codomain.
A relation can be shown in roster form, in set-builder form, or by an arrow diagram.
If n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A × B) = pq and the number of relations from A to B is 2^(pq).
∅ and A × B themselves are also relations from A to B.

ex.q: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. R = {(x, y) : y = x + 1} on A. Write R in roster form; find its domain and range.

topics.rl: An IPL auction sheet relating players to franchises is a relation: domain = players sold, range = teams that bought someone.

rv.summary: A relation R from A to B is any subset of A × B. Its domain is the set of first elements, its range the set of images, and the codomain is B; there are 2^(pq) relations from A to B.
focus: Write a relation in roster form from a rule or an arrow diagram
Find domain, range and codomain, knowing range ⊆ codomain
Check whether a given pair satisfies a relation's rule
Count relations: 2^(pq) when n(A) = p, n(B) = q
remember: Relation from A to B: any subset of A × B
Domain = first elements; range = second elements (images); codomain = B
Number of relations from A to B = 2^(pq)
traps: The range is not always the whole codomain: unused elements of B are not in the range
Not every relation is a function

topics.t: What makes a relation a function
topics.h: A vending machine is a function: press one button and you get exactly one snack. If a button gave you two different snacks at random, it wouldn't be a function!
p: A function f from A to B is a relation in which EVERY element of A has EXACTLY ONE image in B. We write f : A → B.
Test: no element of the domain is left out, and no element appears as a first element in two different pairs.
Two elements of A may share the same image — that is still a function.
A real-valued function has codomain R (or a subset of R). If its domain is also a subset of R, it is a real function.
f(a) is the image of a: substitute a in the rule. E.g. f(x) = x² + 1 gives f(−2) = 5.

ex.q: Is R = {(2, 1), (5, 1), (8, 1), (11, 1), (14, 1)} a function? Find its domain and range.
st: All map to 1 — sharing an image is allowed.

topics.rl: Every Aadhaar number points to exactly one person's record — a function from Aadhaar numbers to residents.

rv.summary: A function f : A → B is a relation in which every element of A has exactly one image in B. Different inputs may share an image, and f(a) is found by substituting a in the rule.
focus: Test a relation: every domain element used, and no element with two images
Find f(a) by substitution and solve f(x) = k
Recognise real-valued and real functions
remember: Function: every element of A has exactly one image in B
Two elements of A may share the same image; it is still a function
f(a) is the image of a: substitute a in the rule
traps: A relation where one input has two outputs (like x = y²) is not a function
B may have elements with no pre-image; that does not stop f being a function

topics.t: Domain and range of real functions
topics.h: A calculator flashes ERROR for √(−4) or 1/0. Finding the domain is just listing every input that does NOT make the calculator complain.
p: Unless stated, the domain of a real function is the largest subset of R for which the formula gives a real value.
Square roots: the expression under √ must be ≥ 0. Fractions: the denominator must not be 0.
Range: the set of all outputs. Work it out from the formula, e.g. x² ≥ 0 so x² + 2 ≥ 2.
From a graph: the domain is the spread of the curve along the x-axis, and the range is its spread along the y-axis.
Examples: √(x − 3) has domain [3, ∞); √(9 − x²) has domain [−3, 3] and range [0, 3].

ex.q: Find the domain of f(x) = (x² + 2x + 1)/(x² − 8x + 12).
st: It is zero at x = 2 and x = 6.
All other real numbers are allowed.

topics.rl: A cab app's function 'fare from distance' has domain 'distances ≥ 0' and range 'fares from the base fare upwards' — negative kilometres make no sense.

rv.summary: The domain of a real function is the largest set of real x for which the formula gives a real value: no negative under √ and no zero denominator. The range is the set of all outputs.
focus: Find domains of square-root and fraction functions
Find ranges using facts like x² ≥ 0 and |x| ≥ 0
Read domain and range from a graph
remember: Under √ the expression must be ≥ 0; a denominator must not be 0
√(x − 3) has domain [3, ∞); √(9 − x²) has domain [−3, 3] and range [0, 3]
Domain: spread of the graph along the x-axis; range: spread along the y-axis
traps: 1/√(x + 2) needs x + 2 > 0 (strict), not ≥ 0
Don't forget both roots: x² − 9 = 0 at x = 3 and x = −3

topics.t: Identity, constant, polynomial and rational functions
topics.h: A photocopier set to 100% is the identity function; a flat-fee parking lot is a constant function. Graphs make these personalities visible.
p: Identity function f(x) = x on R: domain and range R; graph is the line y = x through the origin at 45°.
Constant function f(x) = c: domain R, range {c}; graph is a horizontal line y = c.
Polynomial function: f(x) = a₀ + a₁x + … + aₙxⁿ with real coefficients and n a non-negative integer. y = x² is a U-shaped parabola (range [0, ∞)); y = x³ rises through the origin (range R).
Rational function: f(x)/g(x) of two polynomials, defined where g(x) ≠ 0.
y = 1/x: domain and range R − {0}; the graph has two branches, in the first and third quadrants, never touching the axes.

ex.q: Is f(x) = (x² + 1)/(x − 1) a polynomial function, a rational function or neither? State its domain.
st: Denominator x − 1 is zero at x = 1, which must be excluded.
It is not a polynomial because it does not simplify to one.

topics.rl: Boyle's law PV = constant gives P = k/V, the shape of y = 1/x — which is why pressure in a syringe shoots up as you squeeze the volume small.

rv.summary: Common real functions: identity f(x) = x (range R), constant f(x) = c (range {c}), polynomials such as x² and x³, rational functions p(x)/q(x) defined where q(x) ≠ 0, and 1/x with domain and range R − {0}.
focus: Identify polynomial and rational functions
Find the domain of a rational function by removing zeros of the denominator
Know the graphs and ranges of x, c, x², x³ and 1/x
Evaluate these functions at given points
remember: Identity f(x) = x: domain and range R; constant f(x) = c: range {c}
Polynomial: a₀ + a₁x + … + aₙxⁿ, n a non-negative integer; x² has range [0, ∞), x³ has range R
Rational function f(x)/g(x) is defined where g(x) ≠ 0
y = 1/x: domain and range R − {0}; graph in quadrants I and III
traps: 1/x has a negative power (x⁻¹), so x² + 1/x is not a polynomial
Only zeros of the denominator are removed from the domain, not zeros of the numerator

topics.t: Modulus, signum and greatest integer functions
topics.h: Distance never goes negative, a cricket umpire's signal is 'out, not out or wait', and a parking lot charges for every started hour. Meet |x|, signum and [x].
p: Modulus: |x| = x if x ≥ 0 and −x if x < 0. Domain R, range [0, ∞); graph is a V with vertex at the origin.
Signum: f(x) = 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0 (equal to |x|/x for x ≠ 0). Domain R, range {−1, 0, 1}.
Greatest integer function [x]: the greatest integer less than or equal to x. [2.7] = 2, [−2.7] = −3, [5] = 5.
[x] has domain R and range Z; its graph is a staircase with a filled dot at the left end of each step and a hollow dot at the right.
For −1 ≤ x < 0, [x] = −1; for 0 ≤ x < 1, [x] = 0; and so on.
topics.rl: Indian Railways' fare table rounds a journey of 251–300 km into one slab — that is a step function just like [x].

rv.summary: The modulus |x| gives the distance from 0, the signum function gives 1, 0 or −1 by the sign of x, and the greatest integer function [x] gives the greatest integer ≤ x, with range Z.
focus: Evaluate |x|, signum x and [x], especially for negative numbers
State domain and range: |x| → [0, ∞), signum → {−1, 0, 1}, [x] → Z
Describe the graphs: V shape for |x|, staircase for [x]
Solve simple conditions like [x] = 3 or |x| < 3
remember: |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and −x if x < 0
Signum: 1 if x > 0, 0 if x = 0, −1 if x < 0; equals |x|/x for x ≠ 0
[x] = n for n ≤ x < n + 1
traps: [−4.2] is −5, not −4: go down to the integer on the left
The signum range is {−1, 0, 1}, not the interval [−1, 1]

topics.h: A startup's profit is revenue minus cost: P(x) = R(x) − C(x). Adding, subtracting and dividing functions is everyday business maths.
p: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) and (f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x), on the common domain D_f ∩ D_g.
(fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g; (αf)(x) = α f(x) for a real constant α.
(f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g, excluding points where g(x) = 0.
Piecewise functions use different rules on different intervals; check that overlapping pieces agree.
Difference quotient: [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. For f(x) = x², [f(1.1) − f(1)]/(1.1 − 1) = 0.21/0.1 = 2.1.

ex.q: f(x) = √x and g(x) = x are defined on non-negative reals. Find (f + g)(x), (fg)(x) and (f/g)(x) with domains.
st: f/g = √x/x = 1/√x, but g(0) = 0, so exclude x = 0.

topics.rl: A Mumbai dabbawala's daily earning E(x) = 20x − 150 (₹20 per tiffin, ₹150 fixed cost) is a linear function found from two data points.

rv.summary: Real functions can be added, subtracted, multiplied and divided point by point on their common domain, and for f/g we also remove points where g(x) = 0. Piecewise rules must agree where they overlap.
focus: Compute (f ± g)(a), (fg)(a), (αf)(a) and (f/g)(a)
Find the domain of f/g by removing zeros of g
Check whether a piecewise rule is a well-defined function
Find a linear function from two values
remember: (f ± g)(x) = f(x) ± g(x) and (fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g
(f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) on D_f ∩ D_g, excluding g(x) = 0
(αf)(x) = α f(x)
traps: Don't forget to remove the zeros of g from the domain of f/g
Overlapping pieces of a piecewise rule must give the same value, or it is not a function

topics.t: Angles as rotation: degrees and radians
topics.h: A ceiling fan blade, a Ferris wheel at a Dussehra mela and the hands of a clock all sweep angles far bigger than 90° — so trigonometry must grow up beyond right triangles.
p: In Class 10, trigonometric ratios were defined for acute angles. Now we extend them to angles of any size, and then to any real number.
An angle is the amount of rotation of a ray from its initial side to its terminal side. Anticlockwise rotation gives a positive angle; clockwise gives a negative one.
Degree measure: one full turn = 360°; 1° = 60′ (minutes), 1′ = 60″ (seconds).
Radian measure: the angle at the centre subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius is 1 radian. In general θ = l/r (θ in radians).
Convention: when no unit is written, the angle is in radians. So 'sin 2' means the sine of 2 radians, and θ = π/3 means π/3 radians.

ex.q: An arc of length 18 cm subtends an angle θ at the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm. Find θ.
st: Use θ = l/r with l = 18 cm and r = 6 cm.

topics.rl: An ISRO antenna turning 'through 2 radians' and a cricket ball spinning several full turns both use rotation measure that can exceed 360°.

rv.summary: An angle measures the rotation of a ray from its initial to its terminal side: anticlockwise is positive, clockwise negative. It is measured in degrees (360° per turn) or radians, where θ = l/r.
focus: Give the sign of an angle from the direction of rotation
Use θ = l/r (θ in radians) to find an angle or an arc length
Convert between degrees, minutes and seconds
Read angles with no unit as radians
remember: Anticlockwise rotation: positive angle; clockwise: negative angle
1 radian: angle subtended at the centre by an arc equal to the radius; θ = l/r
No unit written → the angle is in radians
traps: Don't read 'sin 2' as sin 2°: it means 2 radians
Don't use θ in degrees in l = rθ

topics.t: Converting degrees and radians; arc problems
topics.h: A Ferris wheel turning 540 times a minute? That's a centrifuge! Converting revolutions, degrees and radians is daily work for engineers.
p: A full circle is 2π radians = 360°, so π radians = 180°.
Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.
1 radian = 180°/π ≈ 57°16′ (approx.) and 1° = π/180 ≈ 0.01746 radian (approx.).
For degree–minute form, first change minutes to degrees: 47°30′ = 47.5° = 95/2 degrees.
Arc problems use l = rθ (θ in radians). One revolution = 2π radians; when a number is needed, NCERT often uses π = 22/7.

ex.q: Convert −47°30′ into radians.

topics.rl: A Mumbai local's wheel of radius 0.5 m that turns through 2π radians moves the train 2π × 0.5 ≈ 3.14 m — arc length is distance travelled.

rv.summary: Since π radians = 180°, multiply by π/180 to change degrees to radians and by 180/π to change radians to degrees. Arc problems use l = rθ with θ in radians.
focus: Convert degrees (including minutes) to radians and radians to degrees
Solve arc, pendulum and wheel problems with l = rθ
Turn revolutions into radians using 1 revolution = 2π
remember: π radians = 180°; 2π radians = 360°
Degrees → radians: × π/180; radians → degrees: × 180/π
traps: Change minutes to degrees before converting: 47°30′ = 47.5°, not 47.30°
Don't forget that one revolution is 2π radians, not π

topics.t: Trigonometric functions on the unit circle
topics.h: Watch a point riding a circle of radius 1 — its x-coordinate is cos x and its y-coordinate is sin x. Every trig fact follows from that one picture.
p: Take the unit circle centred at O. If the arc from (1, 0) to P has length x (radians), then P = (cos x, sin x). Since P is on the circle, cos²x + sin²x = 1.
tan x = sin x/cos x (cos x ≠ 0), cot x = cos x/sin x (sin x ≠ 0), sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x.
Quadrantal values: sin 0 = 0, sin π/2 = 1, sin π = 0, sin 3π/2 = −1, sin 2π = 0; cos 0 = 1, cos π/2 = 0, cos π = −1, cos 3π/2 = 0, cos 2π = 1.
sin x = 0 exactly when x = nπ; cos x = 0 exactly when x = (2n + 1)π/2, where n is any integer.
Dividing cos²x + sin²x = 1 by cos²x or sin²x: 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x.

ex.q: Find the value of sin²(π/4) + cos²(π/6) − tan²(π/3).

topics.rl: Sound engineers at AIR model a pure tone as y = sin(ωt): the up-and-down motion of a point going round a circle.

rv.summary: On the unit circle, the point reached by an arc of length x from (1, 0) is (cos x, sin x), so cos²x + sin²x = 1. The other four functions are ratios or reciprocals of sin and cos.
focus: Read sin x and cos x as the coordinates of a point on the unit circle
Recall sin and cos at 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 and 2π
Find where sin x = 0, cos x = 0, and where tan, sec, cot and cosec are undefined
Use 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x
remember: P = (cos x, sin x) on the unit circle; cos²x + sin²x = 1
tan x = sin x/cos x, cot x = cos x/sin x, sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x
sin x = 0 when x = nπ; cos x = 0 when x = (2n + 1)π/2
1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x
traps: The point is (cos x, sin x), not (sin x, cos x): cos is the x-coordinate
tan x is undefined where cos x = 0, not where sin x = 0

topics.t: Signs in the quadrants; finding all values from one
topics.h: Know one trig value and the quadrant, and you can unlock all six — like knowing a locker code and the floor number.
p: Quadrant I (0 to π/2): all six functions positive.
Quadrant II (π/2 to π): only sin and cosec positive.
Quadrant III (π to 3π/2): only tan and cot positive.
Quadrant IV (3π/2 to 2π): only cos and sec positive.
Method: use sin²x + cos²x = 1 (or 1 + tan²x = sec²x) to find the size, then fix the sign from the quadrant.

ex.q: If cos x = −12/13 and x lies in the third quadrant, find the other five trigonometric functions.
st: In quadrant III, sin x < 0, so sin x = −5/13.
ex.a: sin x = −5/13, tan x = 5/12, cot x = 12/5, sec x = −13/12, cosec x = −13/5

topics.rl: Navigators reading a compass bearing in the second quadrant know at once that the east–west component (cos) is negative — signs carry direction.

rv.summary: The signs of the trig functions depend on the quadrant: all positive in I, only sin and cosec in II, only tan and cot in III, only cos and sec in IV. Find the size from an identity, then fix the sign.
focus: Recall which functions are positive in each quadrant
Find all six trig values from one value and the quadrant
Use sin²x + cos²x = 1, 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x for the size
remember: Quadrant I: all positive; II: sin, cosec positive
Quadrant III: tan, cot positive; IV: cos, sec positive
Method: find the size from an identity, then choose the sign from the quadrant
traps: Don't drop the sign: the square root gives only the size
In quadrant III both sin and cos are negative, so tan and cot are positive

topics.h: The monsoon returns every year, a pendulum every few seconds, and sin x every 2π. Periodicity lets you tame angles like 765° in one step.
p: sin and cos: domain R, range [−1, 1]. tan: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}, range R. cot: domain R − {nπ}, range R.
sec: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}; cosec: domain R − {nπ}. Both have range R − (−1, 1), i.e. |y| ≥ 1.
sin(2nπ + x) = sin x and cos(2nπ + x) = cos x: period 2π. tan(nπ + x) = tan x and cot(nπ + x) = cot x: period π.
Large angles: remove whole turns (multiples of 360° or 2π) first. sin 765° = sin(720° + 45°) = sin 45° = 1/√2.
Negative angles: cos(−x) = cos x and sin(−x) = −sin x. So cos(−1710°) = cos 1710° = cos(4 × 360° + 270°) = cos 270° = 0.

ex.q: Find sec(−1380°).

topics.rl: The tides at Mumbai's coast follow an approximately periodic pattern, so planners model them with sine curves.

rv.summary: sin and cos have domain R and range [−1, 1]; tan and sec exclude odd multiples of π/2, cot and cosec exclude multiples of π. sin and cos repeat every 2π, tan and cot every π.
focus: State the domain and range of all six trig functions
Reduce large angles by removing whole turns (360° or 2π)
Handle negative angles with cos(−x) = cos x and sin(−x) = −sin x
Use period π for tan and cot
remember: sin, cos: domain R, range [−1, 1]; tan: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}, range R
sec and cosec: range R − (−1, 1), i.e. |y| ≥ 1
Period of sin and cos: 2π; period of tan and cot: π
cos(−x) = cos x; sin(−x) = −sin x
traps: The range of cos x includes −1 and 1: it is [−1, 1], not (−1, 1)
sec x can never be a number between −1 and 1, such as 1/2

topics.h: ECG waves at AIIMS, AC current in your home, and ocean waves — all look like the graph of sin x. Let's read those curves.
p: sin x: increases from 0 to 1 in quadrant I, decreases from 1 to 0 in II, decreases from 0 to −1 in III, increases from −1 to 0 in IV.
cos x: decreases from 1 to 0 in I and from 0 to −1 in II; increases from −1 to 0 in III and from 0 to 1 in IV.
tan x: increases in every quadrant — from 0 to ∞ in I, −∞ to 0 in II, 0 to ∞ in III and −∞ to 0 in IV — with vertical asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2.
Graphs of sin and cos are waves between −1 and 1 with period 2π; the cos graph is the sin graph shifted left by π/2.
cot has asymptotes at x = nπ; sec has asymptotes where cos x = 0 and cosec where sin x = 0, and their graphs never enter the band −1 < y < 1.

ex.q: In which quadrants are both sin x and cos x decreasing?
st: sin decreases in quadrants II and III.
cos decreases in quadrants I and II.
ex.a: Only in the second quadrant (π/2 < x < π)

topics.rl: Household AC supply in India is 230 V at 50 Hz: the voltage traces a sine wave 50 times every second.

rv.summary: sin and cos graphs are waves between −1 and 1 with period 2π, and cos is sin shifted left by π/2. tan increases in every quadrant with asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2; sec and cosec never enter −1 < y < 1.
focus: Describe how sin, cos and tan increase or decrease in each quadrant
Find zeros, maxima and asymptotes from the graphs
Relate the sin and cos graphs by a shift of π/2
remember: sin x: increases 0 → 1 in I, decreases 1 → 0 in II, 0 → −1 in III, increases −1 → 0 in IV
cos x: decreases 1 → 0 in I and 0 → −1 in II; increases −1 → 0 in III and 0 → 1 in IV
tan x increases in every quadrant; asymptotes at x = (2n + 1)π/2
cos x = sin(x + π/2): the sin graph shifted left by π/2
traps: sin x is zero at multiples of π, not at odd multiples of π/2
Don't forget both end points: sin x cuts the x-axis at 0, π and 2π on [0, 2π]

topics.h: Every allied-angle trick — cos(π − x), sin(π/2 + x) — comes out of ONE formula: cos(x + y). Learn it once, and the rest follow.
p: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y. It is proved from the unit circle by equating the distance between two pairs of points on it.
Replace y by −y: cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.
cos(π/2 − x) = sin x, sin(π/2 − x) = cos x; cos(π/2 + x) = −sin x, sin(π/2 + x) = cos x.
cos(π − x) = −cos x, sin(π − x) = sin x; cos(π + x) = −cos x, sin(π + x) = −sin x.
cos(2π − x) = cos x, sin(2π − x) = −sin x.

ex.q: Find cos 15° using cos(x − y).

topics.rl: Phase-shift tricks such as cos(π/2 − x) = sin x are used in electrical engineering to compare AC voltages that are out of step.

rv.summary: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y and cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y. From these come the allied-angle results for π/2 ± x, π ± x and 2π − x.
focus: State and use cos(x + y) and cos(x − y)
Simplify allied angles like π − x, π/2 + x and 2π − x with the correct sign
Find exact values such as cos 15°, cos 105° and cos 330°
Recognise expanded forms like cos A cos B + sin A sin B
remember: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y; cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y
cos(π/2 − x) = sin x, sin(π/2 − x) = cos x; cos(π/2 + x) = −sin x, sin(π/2 + x) = cos x
cos(π − x) = −cos x, sin(π − x) = sin x; cos(π + x) = −cos x, sin(π + x) = −sin x
cos(2π − x) = cos x, sin(2π − x) = −sin x
traps: In cos(x + y) the sign between the terms is '−', the opposite of the sign inside
cos(x + y) is not cos x + cos y

topics.t: sin(x ± y), tan(x ± y) and exact values
topics.h: Your calculator knows sin 15°, but can you get its exact surd value with just 45° and 30°? Sum and difference formulas say yes.
p: sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y; sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y.
tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y), tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y), when the tangents and the result are defined.
cot(x + y) = (cot x cot y − 1)/(cot y + cot x); cot(x − y) = (cot x cot y + 1)/(cot y − cot x).
To prove an identity, expand the compound angles, use allied-angle values, and simplify one side to the other.

ex.q: Find tan(π/4 + x) in terms of tan x.
st: tan(π/4 + x) = (tan π/4 + tan x)/(1 − tan π/4 · tan x).

topics.rl: Surveyors computing the height of a hill in the Western Ghats from two angles of elevation often combine angles with tan(x − y).

rv.summary: sin(x ± y) = sin x cos y ± cos x sin y, and tan(x ± y) = (tan x ± tan y)/(1 ∓ tan x tan y). They give exact values like sin 75° = (√6 + √2)/4 and tan 15° = 2 − √3.
focus: Expand sin(x ± y), tan(x ± y) and cot(x ± y)
Recognise expanded forms and fold them back into one angle
Find exact values of 15°, 75° and 105° type angles
Prove identities by expanding compound angles
remember: sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y; sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y
tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y); tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y)
traps: For sine the sign in the middle matches the sign inside; for cosine it is opposite
In tan(x − y), the denominator is 1 + tan x tan y, not 1 − tan x tan y

topics.h: Put y = x in the sum formulas and you get the double-angle formulas — the most-used identities in Class 11 and 12 calculus.
p: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x = 2 tan x/(1 + tan²x).
cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x = (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x).
tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x).
sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x; cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x; tan 3x = (3 tan x − tan³x)/(1 − 3 tan²x).
Half angles: cos x = 2cos²(x/2) − 1 = 1 − 2sin²(x/2). Take the square root, then choose the sign from the quadrant of x/2.

ex.q: If tan x = −3/4 and x lies in quadrant II, find sin(x/2), cos(x/2) and tan(x/2).
st: x in quadrant II ⇒ π/2 < x < π ⇒ π/4 < x/2 < π/2, so all half-angle values are positive.

topics.rl: The formula sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x tells a cricket coach that a ball thrown at 45° goes farthest (ignoring air resistance), because sin 90° = 1 is the largest.

rv.summary: Double-angle formulas: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x, tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x). Triple and half-angle results follow from them.
focus: Use all forms of sin 2x, cos 2x and tan 2x
Use sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x and cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x
Find half-angle values and choose the sign from the quadrant of x/2
Spot 2 sin x cos x as sin 2x in simplification
remember: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x = 2 tan x/(1 + tan²x)
cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x = (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x)
tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x)
sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x; cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x
traps: The order in cos 3x is reversed: 4 cos³x − 3 cos x, not 3 cos x − 4 cos³x
For half angles, the sign depends on the quadrant of x/2, not of x

topics.h: When two tabla notes of nearly equal pitch play together, you hear 'beats'. The maths behind it is sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x+y)/2) cos((x−y)/2).
p: cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y); −2 sin x sin y = cos(x + y) − cos(x − y).
2 sin x cos y = sin(x + y) + sin(x − y); 2 cos x sin y = sin(x + y) − sin(x − y).
Proving identities: convert sums to products (or products to sums), cancel common factors, then use allied or double-angle results.

ex.q: Prove that (cos 9x + cos 3x)/(sin 9x − sin 3x) = cot 3x.

topics.rl: Radio engineers mix two signals by multiplying them; the product-to-sum formula 2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y) shows the new frequencies that appear.

rv.summary: Sum-to-product formulas turn sin x ± sin y and cos x ± cos y into products of half-sums and half-differences; product-to-sum formulas turn 2 sin x cos y and similar products into sums.
focus: Convert sums of sines and cosines into products
Convert products like 2 sin A cos B into sums
Find exact values such as cos 75° + cos 15° or sin 75° − sin 15°
Simplify quotients by cancelling common factors
remember: sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y); 2 sin x cos y = sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)
traps: Don't forget the minus sign in cos x − cos y = −2 sin(…) sin(…)
Use half-sums (x + y)/2 and half-differences (x − y)/2, not x + y and x − y

topics.t: The imaginary unit i and complex numbers
topics.h: No real number squared gives −1. So mathematicians invented one: i. Today electrical engineers at power grids use it every day.
p: x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, because x² ≥ 0 for every real x. We extend R by a new number i with i² = −1.
A complex number is z = a + ib with a, b real. Re z = a is the real part and Im z = b is the imaginary part. The set of complex numbers is C.
If b = 0, z = a is purely real; if a = 0 and b ≠ 0, z = ib is purely imaginary. So every real number is a complex number.
Equality: a + ib = c + id exactly when a = c AND b = d.
Note: Im z is the real number b, not ib. For z = 3 − 5i, Im z = −5.

ex.q: Find real x and y if (2x + y) + (x + 2)i = 5 + yi.

topics.rl: AC circuit engineers write impedance as Z = R + iX (they often use j for i), with resistance as the real part and reactance as the imaginary part.

rv.summary: A complex number is z = a + ib, where a, b are real and i² = −1; Re z = a and Im z = b. Two complex numbers are equal only when both their real parts and imaginary parts are equal.
focus: Find Re z and Im z, remembering Im z is the real number b
Solve for unknowns by equating real and imaginary parts
Identify purely real and purely imaginary numbers
remember: i² = −1; z = a + ib with a, b real
Re z = a, Im z = b (for 3 − 5i, Im z = −5, not −5i)
a + ib = c + id exactly when a = c and b = d
Every real number a = a + 0i is a complex number
traps: Im z is b, not ib

topics.h: Adding complex numbers is like adding bank balances in two separate accounts — real with real, imaginary with imaginary.
p: (a + ib) + (c + id) = (a + c) + i(b + d).
Properties of addition: closure, commutative z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁, associative, additive identity 0 = 0 + 0i, additive inverse −z = −a − ib.
Subtraction: z₁ − z₂ = z₁ + (−z₂) = (a − c) + i(b − d).
Always simplify the final answer to the standard form a + ib.
Be careful with brackets: −(3 − 2i) = −3 + 2i.

ex.q: Express (1/4 + 3i/4) − (2i + 3/2) in the form a + ib.

topics.rl: Engineers add the impedances of two components in series exactly this way: real parts add and imaginary parts add.

rv.summary: Add or subtract complex numbers by combining real parts with real parts and imaginary parts with imaginary parts. Addition is closed, commutative and associative, with identity 0 and inverse −z.
focus: Add and subtract complex numbers and write the answer as a + ib
Find the additive inverse −z
Name the properties of addition
remember: (a + ib) + (c + id) = (a + c) + i(b + d)
z₁ − z₂ = (a − c) + i(b − d)
Additive identity 0 = 0 + 0i; additive inverse −z = −a − ib

Don't mix real and imaginary parts when collecting terms

topics.h: Multiply out (a + ib)(c + id) like any two brackets — then one tiny rule, i² = −1, does the magic.
p: (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac − bd) + i(ad + bc).
Properties: closure, commutative, associative, multiplicative identity 1 = 1 + 0i, and distributive z₁(z₂ + z₃) = z₁z₂ + z₁z₃.
Identities from real algebra still hold: (z₁ + z₂)² = z₁² + 2z₁z₂ + z₂², (z₁ − z₂)³ = z₁³ − 3z₁²z₂ + 3z₁z₂² − z₂³, z₁² − z₂² = (z₁ + z₂)(z₁ − z₂).
Useful results: (1 + i)² = 2i, (1 − i)² = −2i, (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b².
Always replace i² by −1 and collect real and imaginary parts at the end.
topics.rl: Rotating a phone screen image by 90° is the same as multiplying each point (as a complex number) by i.

rv.summary: Multiply complex numbers like binomials and replace i² by −1: (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac − bd) + i(ad + bc). Multiplication is commutative, associative and distributive, with identity 1.
focus: Multiply complex numbers and simplify to a + ib
Use (1 + i)² = 2i, (1 − i)² = −2i and (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b²
Apply algebraic identities to complex numbers

(a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b²
Multiplicative identity: 1 = 1 + 0i

(a + ib)(a − ib) is a² + b², not a² − b²

topics.t: Powers of i and roots of negative numbers
topics.h: i, −1, −i, 1, i, −1, … The powers of i repeat every four steps — like the four seasons, or the four innings of a Test match.
p: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, and then the pattern repeats.
For any integer k: i^(4k) = 1, i^(4k+1) = i, i^(4k+2) = −1, i^(4k+3) = −i. Divide the power by 4 and use the remainder.
Negative powers: 1/i = −i, so i^(−n) = 1/iⁿ. For example i^(−3) = 1/(−i) = i.
Square root of a negative real: √(−a) = i√a for a > 0, e.g. √(−9) = 3i.
√a·√b = √(ab) is FALSE when both a and b are negative: √(−4)·√(−9) = (2i)(3i) = −6, not √36 = 6.

ex.q: Simplify i⁹ + i¹⁹.

topics.rl: Digital signal processors in mobile phones use the repeating cycle 1, i, −1, −i to rotate signals in steps of 90°.

rv.summary: Powers of i repeat in a cycle of four: i, −1, −i, 1. Divide the power by 4 and use the remainder; for a > 0, √(−a) = i√a, but √a·√b = √(ab) fails when both are negative.
focus: Simplify large positive and negative powers of i
Write square roots of negative numbers using i
Avoid the wrong rule √a·√b = √(ab) for two negative numbers
Use the fact that four consecutive powers of i add to 0
remember: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1
1/i = −i; √(−a) = i√a for a > 0
traps: For negative powers, find iⁿ first and then take its reciprocal

topics.t: Reciprocal and division of complex numbers
topics.h: Dividing by 3 + 4i looks scary — until you multiply top and bottom by 3 − 4i and the i disappears from the denominator.
p: For z = a + ib ≠ 0, z·z̄ = (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b² = |z|², a real number.
Multiplicative inverse: z⁻¹ = 1/z = z̄/|z|² = (a − ib)/(a² + b²).
Division: z₁/z₂ = z₁ · (1/z₂) = z₁z̄₂/|z₂|², for z₂ ≠ 0.
In practice: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
Check: z · z⁻¹ should equal 1.

ex.q: Find the multiplicative inverse of 4 − 3i.

topics.rl: Electrical engineers find current I = V/Z by dividing a voltage by a complex impedance, using exactly this conjugate trick.

rv.summary: For z = a + ib ≠ 0, z·z̄ = a² + b² is real, so 1/z = z̄/|z|² = (a − ib)/(a² + b²). To divide, multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
focus: Find the multiplicative inverse of a complex number
Divide complex numbers using the conjugate of the denominator
Find Re and Im of a quotient or reciprocal
remember: z·z̄ = (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b² = |z|²
z⁻¹ = z̄/|z|² = (a − ib)/(a² + b²)
z₁/z₂ = z₁z̄₂/|z₂|², z₂ ≠ 0
traps: The reciprocal of 2 + 5i is not 1/2 + (1/5)i
Divide by a² + b², not a² − b²

topics.h: The modulus of a complex number is its 'size' — the straight-line distance from the origin, just like how far a drone is from its launch pad.
p: For z = a + ib: modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) and conjugate z̄ = a − ib.
|z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| and |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂| (z₂ ≠ 0).
Conjugates: (z₁ + z₂)‾ = z̄₁ + z̄₂, (z₁ − z₂)‾ = z̄₁ − z̄₂, (z₁z₂)‾ = z̄₁z̄₂, (z₁/z₂)‾ = z̄₁/z̄₂.
|z̄| = |z| and z + z̄ = 2 Re z, z − z̄ = 2i Im z.
Shortcut: to find the modulus of a product or quotient, find each modulus separately — no need to multiply out.
topics.rl: GPS apps calculate the straight-line distance between two places with the same √(a² + b²) idea that gives the modulus.

rv.summary: For z = a + ib, the modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²) and the conjugate is z̄ = a − ib. Moduli multiply and divide (|z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|), and conjugates pass through +, −, × and ÷.
focus: Find |z| and z̄
Find the modulus of a product or quotient by taking each modulus separately
Use z + z̄ = 2 Re z, z − z̄ = 2i Im z and |z̄| = |z|
remember: |z| = √(a² + b²); z̄ = a − ib
|z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|; |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|
(z₁z₂)‾ = z̄₁z̄₂; |z̄| = |z|
z + z̄ = 2 Re z; z − z̄ = 2i Im z
traps: |a + ib| is √(a² + b²), not a + b
To find the conjugate of a product, first simplify it to a + ib, then change the sign of the imaginary part

topics.h: Complex numbers live on a map! Real part across, imaginary part up — and suddenly modulus is distance and conjugate is a mirror.
p: z = x + iy is plotted as the point (x, y). This plane is the complex plane or Argand plane.
The x-axis is the real axis (points a + 0i) and the y-axis is the imaginary axis (points 0 + ib). E.g. 2 + 4i is (2, 4) and −3 + i is (−3, 1) in quadrant II.
|z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin.
The conjugate z̄ = x − iy is the point (x, −y): the reflection of z in the real axis.
Syllabus note: polar form, square roots of complex numbers and complex roots of quadratic equations are not part of the current CBSE exam syllabus for this chapter.

ex.q: If (x + iy)³ = u + iv, write u and v in terms of x and y, and check with x = 1, y = 2.

topics.rl: Engineers and game designers represent 2-D positions and rotations compactly as complex numbers in a plane.

rv.summary: In the Argand plane, z = x + iy is the point (x, y): the x-axis is the real axis and the y-axis is the imaginary axis. |z| is the distance from the origin, and z̄ is the reflection of z in the real axis.
focus: Plot complex numbers and name their quadrants
Find |z| as a distance from the origin
Interpret z̄ as a reflection in the real axis
Solve mixed problems by simplifying to x + iy and equating parts
remember: z = x + iy ↔ point (x, y); x-axis = real axis, y-axis = imaginary axis
|z| = √(x² + y²) = distance from the origin
z̄ = x − iy is the point (x, −y): reflection in the real axis
traps: The conjugate reflects in the real axis, not the imaginary axis
Simplify z to the form x + iy before plotting it

topics.h: You have ₹200 for samosas at ₹15 each. You can't spend MORE than you have — and that 'not more than' is an inequality: 15x ≤ 200.
p: Real life is full of limits: a budget, a speed limit, a minimum attendance. These are written as inequalities.
Two expressions compared with <, >, ≤ or ≥ form an inequality. 3 < 5 is numerical; x < 5 or 2x + 3y ≥ 6 is literal (it has variables).
Strict inequalities use < or >; slack (non-strict) ones use ≤ or ≥.
ax + b < 0 (a ≠ 0) is a linear inequality in one variable; ax + by ≥ c is linear in two variables; ax² + bx + c > 0 (a ≠ 0) is quadratic, not linear.
Turning words into symbols: 'at least' → ≥, 'at most / cannot exceed / not more than' → ≤, 'more than' → >, 'less than' → <.

ex.q: Ravi earns ₹30,000 a month and spends ₹x on rent and ₹12,000 on everything else. Write the condition that his spending cannot exceed his income.
st: 'Cannot exceed' means 'less than or equal to'.

topics.rl: RBI's inflation target band of 4% ± 2% is an inequality: 2 ≤ inflation (%) ≤ 6.

rv.summary: An inequality compares two expressions with <, >, ≤ or ≥. Strict ones use < or >, slack ones use ≤ or ≥, and word limits like 'at least' and 'at most' become ≥ and ≤.
focus: Tell strict from slack inequalities, and numerical from literal ones
Classify inequalities as linear in one or two variables, or quadratic
Translate word conditions ('at least', 'at most', 'more than') into symbols
remember: Strict: < or >; slack (non-strict): ≤ or ≥
ax + b < 0 (a ≠ 0): linear in one variable; ax + by ≥ c: linear in two variables; ax² + bx + c > 0 (a ≠ 0): quadratic
'At least' → ≥; 'at most / cannot exceed / not more than' → ≤; 'more than' → >; 'less than' → <
traps: 'At most' includes equality: use ≤, not <
An inequality with x² or a product like xy is not linear

topics.h: Solving an inequality is like solving an equation — with ONE trap: multiply or divide by a negative number and the sign flips.
p: A solution is a value that makes the inequality true; the set of all solutions is the solution set.
Rule 1: the same number may be added to (or subtracted from) both sides without changing the sign.
Rule 2: both sides may be multiplied or divided by the same POSITIVE number without changing the sign; for a NEGATIVE number, the sign reverses (< becomes >).
The answer depends on the allowed values: 30x < 200 gives x < 20/3, so x ∈ {1, 2, …, 6} if x ∈ N, x ∈ {…, 5, 6} if x ∈ Z, and all real x < 20/3 if x ∈ R.
With fractions, multiply through by the LCM of the denominators (a positive number) first; open brackets carefully.

ex.q: Solve x/4 > x/3 + 1 for real x.
st: Multiply by −1 and reverse the sign: x < −12.

topics.rl: A Delhi metro card has ₹480. Each trip costs ₹40 and at least ₹100 must stay on the card: 480 − 40n ≥ 100 gives n ≤ 9.5, so at most 9 trips.

rv.summary: Solve a linear inequality like an equation, but if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the sign. The final solution set depends on whether x is natural, integer or real.
focus: Solve linear inequalities, reversing the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Clear fractions by multiplying by the positive LCM first
Write the solution set for x ∈ N, x ∈ Z or x ∈ R
remember: Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the sign
Multiplying or dividing by a positive number keeps the sign; by a negative number reverses it
The solution set depends on the allowed values (N, Z or R)
traps: Don't forget to flip < to > when dividing by a negative number
Don't include numbers that are not allowed, like 0 or negatives, when x ∈ N

topics.t: Number line, intervals, systems and double inequalities
topics.h: A medicine is safe between 2 °C and 8 °C — not one, but two conditions at once. Systems and double inequalities handle exactly that.
p: On the number line, a filled (dark) circle means the end point is included (≤, ≥); a hollow circle means it is excluded (<, >).
Write answers in interval notation: x ≥ 2 → [2, ∞); x < −1 → (−∞, −1); −3 < x ≤ 5 → (−3, 5].
A system of inequalities: solve each one, then take the common part (intersection) of the solution sets.
A double inequality like a ≤ (px + q)/r ≤ b: do the same operation to all three parts; if you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse BOTH signs.

ex.q: Solve the system 2x + 1 > x − 3 and 3x − 2 ≤ 7, and write the answer as an interval.

topics.rl: Vaccines in India's cold chain must stay between 2 °C and 8 °C: the double inequality 2 ≤ T ≤ 8, drawn as a closed segment on a thermometer.

rv.summary: Show solutions on the number line with filled circles for ≤, ≥ and hollow circles for <, >, and write them as intervals. For a system, take the common part; for a double inequality, do each step to all three parts.
focus: Draw solutions on a number line with filled or hollow circles
Write solutions in interval notation
Solve systems of inequalities by intersecting the solution sets
Solve double inequalities, reversing both signs when dividing by a negative number
remember: Filled circle: end point included (≤, ≥); hollow circle: excluded (<, >)
System: solve each inequality, then take the intersection
Double inequality: apply each operation to all three parts
traps: In a double inequality, reverse BOTH signs when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
A system with no common values has no solution (∅); don't report one of the separate answers

topics.t: Word problems: marks, integers and lengths
topics.h: 'How much do I need in the last test to get 70% overall?' — the question every Class 11 student asks. Inequalities answer it.
p: Step 1: name the unknown. Step 2: translate the condition into an inequality. Step 3: solve. Step 4: keep only answers that make sense (whole numbers, positive lengths, etc.).
Average condition: (sum of scores)/(number of tests) ≥ target.
Consecutive odd (or even) integers: x and x + 2. Consecutive integers: x and x + 1.
Lengths: express every side or piece in terms of one variable; perimeter or total length gives the inequality.
Temperature: C = (5/9)(F − 32). A range in °F converts to a range in °C by applying the formula to both ends.

ex.q: Aman scored 68 and 75 in the first two unit tests. What is the minimum he must score in the third test to have an average of at least 72?
st: Let the third score be x.

topics.rl: JEE and NEET aspirants use the same average-target logic when planning mock-test scores for the last few weeks.

rv.summary: For word problems: name the unknown, turn the condition into an inequality, solve it, and keep only sensible answers. Typical cases are averages of marks, consecutive integers, lengths and temperature ranges.
focus: Translate average, consecutive-number and length conditions into inequalities
Solve and keep only sensible values (whole numbers, positive lengths)
Convert a °F range to °C using C = (5/9)(F − 32)
remember: Average: (sum of scores)/(number of tests) ≥ target
Consecutive odd or even integers: x and x + 2; consecutive integers: x and x + 1
C = (5/9)(F − 32), applied to both ends of a range
traps: Don't stop at the algebra: check the answer fits all the conditions in the question
Multiplying by a positive number such as 3 keeps the sign; don't reverse it

topics.h: A chemist must keep an acid solution between 6% and 8% strength. How much weaker solution can she pour in? That's a double inequality.
p: Mixture problems: amount of pure substance = concentration × volume. Track the total pure substance and the total volume.
Concentration of the mixture = (total pure substance)/(total volume); put it between the given limits.
Solve the two halves of the double inequality separately (or together), then combine.
IQ formula: IQ = (MA/CA) × 100, where MA is mental age and CA is chronological age.
If IQ lies between two values, multiply the whole inequality by CA/100 (positive) to get the range of MA.

ex.q: 500 L of a 10% acid solution is mixed with x L of a 4% acid solution. For the mixture to be more than 6% but less than 8% acid, find x.

topics.rl: Pharmacists at a Jan Aushadhi store dilute antiseptic stock solutions so the final strength stays within the safe band printed on the label.

rv.summary: In mixture problems, pure substance = concentration × volume, and the mixture's concentration is total pure substance over total volume. With IQ = (MA/CA) × 100, multiply the IQ range by CA/100 to get the mental-age range.
focus: Write the total pure substance and total volume of a mixture
Set the mixture's concentration between given limits and solve
Use IQ = (MA/CA) × 100 to move between IQ and mental-age ranges
remember: Pure substance = concentration × volume
Concentration of mixture = (total pure substance)/(total volume)
IQ = (MA/CA) × 100
traps: Volume is positive, so multiplying by it keeps the inequality sign
Don't add percentages directly: work with the amounts of pure substance

topics.h: 3 kurtas and 4 pairs of jeans: how many outfits? You don't need to list them — 3 × 4 = 12. That multiplication is the most powerful idea in counting.
p: Counting by listing is slow and error-prone; the counting principles let us count arrangements and selections without listing.
Multiplication principle: if one event can happen in m ways and, after it, another can happen in n ways, the two together can happen in m × n ways.
It extends to any number of events: m × n × p × … ways.
Use it for building codes, numbers, number plates and signals position by position: fill each place in turn and multiply the choices.
Example: signals made by hoisting 2 of 4 different flags one below the other: 4 × 3 = 12 signals.

ex.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if no digit is repeated?

topics.rl: An Indian vehicle number like MH 12 AB 1234 is built position by position; the multiplication principle tells the RTO how many plates a series can issue.

rv.summary: The multiplication principle: if one event can happen in m ways and then another in n ways, together they can happen in m × n ways. Fill positions one by one and multiply the choices.
focus: Apply the multiplication principle to menus, codes, signals and tosses
Fill places one at a time, reducing the choices when items cannot be reused
Explain why we multiply rather than add
remember: Multiplication principle: m ways then n ways → m × n ways
Extends to more events: m × n × p × …
Signals with 2 of 4 different flags: 4 × 3 = 12
traps: Don't add the choices for successive steps: multiply them
When an item cannot be reused, the choices drop by one at each step

topics.h: A 4-digit UPI PIN can repeat digits; a lucky-draw ticket with all-different digits cannot. That one rule changes the count completely.
p: With repetition allowed, every position has the full number of choices: 4-digit PINs from 0–9 = 10⁴ = 10,000.
Without repetition, the choices drop by one at each step: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040.
Fill restricted positions FIRST (e.g. the units digit for even numbers, the first digit that cannot be 0).
Words from letters: 'word' means any arrangement of letters, with or without meaning.
Example: 4-letter codes from the first 10 letters of the alphabet without repetition: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040.

ex.q: How many 4-digit even numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition?
st: Units digit: 2 or 4 → 2 choices (fill it first).

topics.rl: Mobile numbers in India have 10 digits starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9 — counting with repetition explains why TRAI never runs out quickly.

rv.summary: With repetition allowed, every position has the full set of choices; without repetition the choices drop by one at each step. Always fill restricted positions, such as the first or last digit, first.
focus: Count codes, PINs and numbers with and without repetition
Handle 'first digit cannot be 0' and 'even/odd' restrictions by filling those places first
Treat 'words' as any arrangement of letters
remember: With repetition: 4-digit PINs from 0–9 = 10⁴ = 10,000
Without repetition: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040
Fill restricted positions first
traps: The first digit of a number cannot be 0
Don't use repetition counts (like 5³) when the question says no repetition

topics.h: In how many ways can 11 players walk out in a line before a World Cup match? 11! = 39,916,800. Factorials grow FAST.
p: A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a definite order.
Number of permutations of n different objects taken r at a time (no repetition): nPr = n(n − 1)(n − 2)…(n − r + 1) = n!/(n − r)!, 0 ≤ r ≤ n.
Derivation: fill r places one by one — n choices, then n − 1, …, then n − r + 1 — and multiply.
With repetition allowed, the number of arrangements of n objects taken r at a time is nʳ.

ex.q: Evaluate 8!/(6! × 2!).

topics.rl: The BCCI's selection panel ranking 3 players for 'captain, vice-captain, wicketkeeper' from 15 is ¹⁵P₃ = 2730 ordered choices.

rv.summary: A permutation is an ordered arrangement. The number of arrangements of n different objects taken r at a time is nPr = n!/(n − r)!, where n! = 1 × 2 × … × n and 0! = 1; with repetition it is nʳ.
focus: Evaluate factorials and expressions like 8!/(6! 2!)
Compute nPr = n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1)
Use nʳ when repetition is allowed
Simplify n!/(n − r)! algebraically
remember: With repetition: nʳ arrangements
traps: Factorials don't add: 3! + 4! ≠ 7!
0! is 1, not 0

topics.h: Swap the two Os in 'BALLOON' and nothing changes. That's why arrangements of alike letters need dividing, not just multiplying.
p: If p of n objects are alike (and the rest different), the number of arrangements of all n is n!/p!.
Reason: swapping the p alike objects among themselves (p! ways) gives the same arrangement, so n! counts each one p! times.
If p₁, p₂, …, pₖ objects are alike of k kinds, the number of arrangements is n!/(p₁! p₂! … pₖ!).
Example: MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters with I × 4, S × 4, P × 2: 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = 34,650.
ALLAHABAD has 9 letters with A × 4, L × 2: 9!/(4! 2!) = 7560.

ex.q: How many different words can be formed from the letters of BALLOON?
st: 7 letters: B, A, L, L, O, O, N.
L appears 2 times, O appears 2 times.

topics.rl: A DNA sequence of 10 bases with 4 A, 3 G, 2 C and 1 T can be arranged in 10!/(4! 3! 2! 1!) = 12,600 ways — biotech labs count exactly like this.

rv.summary: If p of n objects are alike, the n objects can be arranged in n!/p! ways; with several groups of alike objects, divide n! by the factorial of each group size: n!/(p₁! p₂! … pₖ!).
focus: Count arrangements of words with repeated letters
Count arrangements of identical coloured objects or repeated digits
Explain why we divide by p!
remember: p alike out of n: n!/p! arrangements
Several kinds alike: n!/(p₁! p₂! … pₖ!)
traps: Count each repeated letter carefully before dividing
Don't divide by 1! for single letters as if it changed anything; only repeats matter

topics.h: 'Vowels must sit together', 'the number must be divisible by 5' — exam questions love conditions. The trick: handle the condition first.
p: Vowels together: glue them into one block, arrange the block with the other letters, then arrange the vowels inside the block.
Vowels never together = (all arrangements) − (arrangements with all vowels together), when the condition is 'not all together'.
Fixed positions: if a word must start or end with given letters, place them first, then arrange the rest.
Divisibility: even → last digit even; divisible by 5 → last digit 0 or 5; divisible by 10 → last digit 0. Fill that place first.
To find n from a relation like nP5 = 20 nP3, write both sides as products and cancel: (n − 3)(n − 4) = 20, so n = 8.

ex.q: In how many arrangements of the letters of DAUGHTER are the vowels together? In how many are they not all together?
st: DAUGHTER has 8 different letters; vowels A, U, E.
Glue the vowels: 5 consonants + 1 block = 6 units → 6! = 720.

topics.rl: Seating plans at a wedding ('keep the family of the bride together') are vowels-together problems in disguise.

rv.summary: For conditions: glue items that must be together into one block, subtract 'together' cases from the total for 'not all together', and place fixed or restricted positions first. Solve nPr equations by cancelling common factors.
focus: Count arrangements with items kept together (block method)
Count 'not all together' as total minus together
Handle fixed first/last letters and divisibility conditions
Solve equations such as ⁿP₅ = 20 × ⁿP₃
remember: Together: treat the group as one block, then multiply by the arrangements inside the block
Not all together = total − all together
Divisible by 10 → last digit 0; even → last digit even; fill that place first
traps: Don't forget to arrange the letters inside the block
'Not together' is total minus together, not the block count again

topics.h: Choosing 3 friends for a trip to Goa is a combination — the order you pick them doesn't matter. Ranking them 1st, 2nd, 3rd would be a permutation.
p: A combination is a selection where order does not matter.
nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), 0 ≤ r ≤ n. Each selection of r objects can be arranged in r! ways, so nPr = r! × nCr.
nC0 = nCn = 1, and nCr = nC(n − r) (choosing r to take = choosing n − r to leave).
If nCa = nCb, then a = b or a + b = n.
Pascal's rule: nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr.

ex.q: If ⁿC₇ = ⁿC₅, find ⁿC₂.

topics.rl: A cricket selector picking 15 players from 25 probables for a squad is choosing a combination: ²⁵C₁₅ = 3,268,760 squads are possible.

rv.summary: A combination is a selection where order does not matter: nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Useful facts: nPr = r! × nCr, nCr = nC(n − r), and Pascal's rule nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr.
focus: Evaluate nCr
Solve equations like ⁿC₂ = 45 or ⁿCa = ⁿCb
Use nCr = nC(n − r), Pascal's rule and nPr = r! × nCr
Decide when a problem is a selection (combination) rather than an arrangement
remember: nPr = r! × nCr
nC0 = nCn = 1; nCr = nC(n − r); if nCa = nCb then a = b or a + b = n
Pascal's rule: nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr
traps: Committees and selections are combinations: don't use nPr when order does not matter
In Pascal's rule, n goes up by 1 but r stays the larger of the two

topics.h: The school quiz team needs 2 boys and 3 girls, with at least one Class 12 student. Questions like this mix combinations with 'at least' and 'at most'.
p: Separate groups: choose from each group and multiply, e.g. 2 boys from 7 and 3 girls from 5: ⁷C₂ × ⁵C₃.
'At least' / 'at most': add the cases, or use total − unwanted cases (e.g. at least 1 girl = total − no girls).
Cards: a deck has 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 4 aces, 12 face cards (J, Q, K). Exactly one ace in 4 cards: ⁴C₁ × ⁴⁸C₃.
Lines through n points (no three collinear): ⁿC₂. Triangles: ⁿC₃. Diagonals of an n-gon: ⁿC₂ − n.
Read 'exactly', 'at least' and 'at most' carefully — they decide which cases to add.

ex.q: A committee of 5 is to be formed from 6 boys and 5 girls with exactly 3 boys and 2 girls. In how many ways?

topics.rl: A Ranji Trophy squad selection ('at least 4 bowlers, at most 2 wicket-keepers') is solved with exactly these case-by-case combinations.

rv.summary: For selections from separate groups, choose from each group and multiply. Handle 'at least' or 'at most' by adding cases or by total minus unwanted cases; geometry counts use ⁿC₂ for lines, ⁿC₃ for triangles and ⁿC₂ − n for diagonals.
focus: Form committees from separate groups (boys/girls) and multiply
Solve 'at least' and 'exactly' problems
Count card selections from a 52-card deck
Count lines, triangles and diagonals from points
remember: Separate groups: ⁷C₂ × ⁵C₃ style products
At least 1 girl = total − no girls
Deck: 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 4 aces, 12 face cards (J, Q, K)
Lines: ⁿC₂; triangles: ⁿC₃; diagonals of an n-gon: ⁿC₂ − n
traps: Read 'exactly', 'at least' and 'at most' carefully before counting
Diagonals are ⁿC₂ minus the n sides, not ⁿC₂

topics.h: Make 5-letter words from DAUGHTER using 2 vowels and 3 consonants: first CHOOSE the letters, then ARRANGE them. Most hard problems are two easy ones glued together.
p: Mixed problems: number of ways = (ways to select) × (ways to arrange the selected objects).
Example: 2 vowels from 3 and 3 consonants from 5 in DAUGHTER, then arrange 5 letters: ³C₂ × ⁵C₃ × 5! = 3600.
Dictionary (rank) problems: list letters alphabetically; count words that begin with each smaller letter, then fix letters one by one.
Rows with restrictions: place the restricted group first (e.g. girls in even places), then the rest.
Always check whether letters are distinct; repeated letters need division by factorials.

ex.q: If all arrangements of RANK are listed in dictionary order, what is the rank of RANK?
st: Letters in order: A, K, N, R.
Words starting with A, K, N: 3 × 3! = 18.
Starting with R: next letter A; remaining K, N give RAKN (19th), RANK (20th).

topics.rl: Password-strength meters estimate how many passwords an attacker must try — select characters, then arrange them.

rv.summary: Mixed problems: first select (nCr), then arrange (r!), and multiply. For dictionary rank, count all words that come before the given word and add 1.
focus: Solve select-then-arrange problems with letters, digits and books
Find the rank of a word in dictionary order
Place restricted groups first, then the rest
remember: Ways = (ways to select) × (ways to arrange the selected objects)
DAUGHTER, 2 vowels + 3 consonants: ³C₂ × ⁵C₃ × 5! = 3600
Rank = (number of words before it) + 1
traps: Don't stop after selecting: remember to arrange the chosen objects if order matters
List the letters alphabetically before counting words for a rank

topics.t: Patterns in powers and Pascal's triangle
topics.h: Can you find 98⁵ without multiplying 98 by itself five times? A triangle of numbers known in India as Meru Prastaara, centuries before Pascal, makes it easy.
p: Repeated multiplication of big powers like (98)⁵ or (a + b)ⁿ is slow; we want a formula.
(a + b)⁰ = 1, (a + b)¹ = a + b, (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³, (a + b)⁴ = a⁴ + 4a³b + 6a²b² + 4ab³ + b⁴.
The coefficients form Pascal's triangle: each row starts and ends with 1, and every inner entry is the sum of the two entries just above it.
The entries of row n are ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, …, ⁿCₙ — Pascal's rule ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ is exactly 'add the two above'.

ex.q: Use Pascal's triangle to expand (a + b)⁵.
st: Powers of a fall 5 → 0; powers of b rise 0 → 5.

topics.rl: Counting Sanskrit verse metres in Pingala's Chhandaḥśāstra led to this pattern; the commentator Halayudha (10th century CE) described it as Meru Prastaara, long before Pascal.

rv.summary: The coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ form Pascal's triangle: each row starts and ends with 1, and each inner entry is the sum of the two entries above it. Row n is ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, …, ⁿCₙ.
focus: Build rows of Pascal's triangle up to row 6
Read coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ from the right row
Link the triangle to ⁿCᵣ and Pascal's rule
Know that row n has n + 1 entries adding to 2ⁿ
remember: Each inner entry = sum of the two entries just above it
Row n entries: ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, …, ⁿCₙ; Pascal's rule ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ
traps: Count rows from 0: the top 1 is row 0, so (a + b)⁶ uses row 6, which has 7 entries
The 3rd entry of row 7 is ⁷C₂, not ⁷C₃

topics.h: One formula expands (a + b)ⁿ for every positive integer n — no matter how big. That's the binomial theorem.
p: (a + b)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ aⁿ + ⁿC₁ aⁿ⁻¹ b + ⁿC₂ aⁿ⁻² b² + … + ⁿCₙ bⁿ, for any positive integer n.
Why: (a + b)ⁿ is n brackets multiplied. A term aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ appears once for every way of choosing b from r of the n brackets — ⁿCᵣ ways.
There are n + 1 terms. Powers of a fall from n to 0, powers of b rise from 0 to n, and in each term the indices add up to n.
The numbers ⁿCᵣ are the binomial coefficients; they read the same from both ends because ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.
Syllabus note: the general-term and middle-term formulas are not part of the current CBSE syllabus for this chapter.

ex.q: Expand (x + 2)⁴ using the binomial theorem.

topics.rl: Actuaries at LIC use binomial expansions to estimate probabilities of many independent events, like several policies maturing together.

rv.summary: Binomial theorem: (a + b)ⁿ = ⁿC₀aⁿ + ⁿC₁aⁿ⁻¹b + … + ⁿCₙbⁿ for any positive integer n. There are n + 1 terms, the powers of a fall, the powers of b rise, and in each term they add to n.
focus: Expand (a + b)ⁿ for small n, including numbers like (x + 2)⁴
Find a specific coefficient using ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ
Count the terms and match powers that add to n
Use the symmetry ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ
remember: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, r = 0 to n
n + 1 terms; in each term the powers of a and b add up to n
ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ (coefficients read the same from both ends)
